1.title: Hypothesis testing fundamentals
elements: para

Hypothesis definition. A hypothesis is a statement about a population parameter that you intend to test. It consists of a null hypothesis (H₀) and an alternative hypothesis (H₁), and you select a test statistic from the sample to evaluate the claim
para

Null and alternative forms. The null hypothesis is written with an equality sign (e.g., H₀: μ = μ₀) while the alternative hypothesis uses an inequality without the equals sign (e.g., H₁: μ > μ₀). No equals sign appears in H₁
para
Type I and II errors. A Type I error occurs when H₀ is true but we reject it; a Type II error occurs when H₀ is false but we fail to reject it
para
Error interpretation. Both represent errors of judgment about the ground truth
para

Alpha and confidence level. Alpha is the chosen significance level, typically 0.05, which corresponds to a 95 % confidence level; a smaller alpha such as 0.01 gives a 99 % confidence level. The confidence level is the complement of the tail probability that we are willing to accept when rejecting the null hypothesis
para

Test types and distributions. A hypothesis test may involve normal, t, F, or chi‑square distributions, but for the remainder of this lecture we restrict attention to the simple normal distribution. The choice between a two‑tail and a single‑tail test depends on the form of the alternative hypothesis
para

Null hypothesis setup. Under a given null hypothesis we specify the parameter value (denoted φ) and then formulate the alternative; for a two‑tail test the alternative is φ≠φ₀, while for a one‑tail test it is φ>φ₀ or φ<φ₀. Rejecting the hypothesis therefore means rejecting the null hypothesis when the test statistic is too large or too small
para

Sampling distribution of the statistic. The sampling distribution of a test statistic is the distribution of that statistic over many repeated samples from the same population. For a normal test statistic the sampling distribution is itself normal, with mean μ equal to the population parameter under the null hypothesis and standard deviation σ equal to the population standard deviation divided by the square root of the sample size
para

Decision rule for a two‑tail test. In a two‑tail test we reject the null hypothesis if the observed statistic falls beyond the critical values in either tail of the standard normal curve; that is, if the statistic is too large (right tail) or too small (left tail)
para

Z‑score construction. The Z‑score is the sample statistic minus the population mean divided by the population standard deviation, Z = (\bar X - μ)/σ. Because the sampling distribution of \bar X has mean μ, this standardises the statistic to a standard normal variable with mean zero and unit variance
para
Rejection rule. If the computed Z lies outside this interval, the null hypothesis is rejected
para
Critical region. The 95% area of the standard normal distribution defines the critical region for a two‑sided test
para
Decision rule. The decision rule at a 0.05 significance level uses the critical values –1.96 and +1.96 – so that if the computed Z lies beyond these bounds, the null hypothesis is rejected
para

Rejection region. The rejection region consists of the extreme right and left tails of the standard normal distribution; if the test statistic falls in either tail, the null hypothesis is rejected. The area in each tail corresponds to the chosen significance level, 2.5% for 0.05 and 0.5% for 0.01
para

Mean and standard deviation. For a binomial experiment with N=64 trials and success probability p=0.5, the null hypothesis assumes a fair coin. The mean under H₀ is μ=Np=64·0.5=32 and the standard deviation is σ=√(Npq)=√(64·0.5·0.5)=4
para
Z‑score formula. The Z‑score for an observed number of heads X is computed as Z=(X−μ)/σ, which here becomes Z=(X−32)/4
example
Example (Finding the critical X values):  Steps: X−32 = 1.96·4 → X = 1.96·4 + 32 = 39.84 (upper critical value); X−32 = −1.96·4 → X = −1.96·4 + 32 = 24.16 (lower critical value).
para
Critical value calculation. The rejection region is defined by z values beyond ±1.96, so the null hypothesis is rejected if the observed X lies outside 24.16 to 39.84
para

Acceptance region. If the observed number of heads lies between 25 and 39, inclusive, the null hypothesis is not rejected and is accepted. The boundaries 24.16 and 39.84 are rounded to the nearest integers, giving 25 and 39 as the practical limits
para
Effect of alpha on CI. When the significance level (α) is decreased, the corresponding confidence level increases, which widens the confidence interval to accommodate a larger error margin
para
Company claim on mean weight. The company asserts that the mean net weight of its potato wafer bags is 454 g, although individual bags may vary slightly above or below this value
para
Quality‑assurance testing. The quality‑assurance team periodically performs hypothesis tests to decide whether the packaging machine is working properly or not
para

Null hypothesis definition. The null hypothesis is the statement that the mean weight of the product is 4.54 grams, i.e., the packaging machine is operating correctly. The alternative hypothesis states that the mean weight is not equal to 4.54 grams, indicating a malfunction
para
Two‑tailed test. For a two‑tailed test the critical region is split into two parts, one in the lower tail and one in the upper tail
para
Rejection rule. The rejection rule is: reject H0 when z < zc1 or z > zc2
para

Test setup. A 95 % confidence hypothesis test is planned to assess whether eating walnuts makes children smarter. A random sample of twelve children is selected and given walnuts for one year before their intelligence scores are measured
para
t‑test selection. When the population standard deviation is unknown and the sample size is small, the appropriate test is the t‑test
para
Sample standard deviation. The sample standard deviation is calculated by taking the square root of the sum of squared deviations from the mean, divided by the sample size minus one
para

Test statistic formula. The test statistic is calculated as (x̄−μ)/(σ/√n), where x̄ is the sample mean, μ is the hypothesised population mean, σ is the sample standard deviation, and n is the sample size. In the example the null hypothesis sets μ = 100, the observed sample mean is 106, the standard deviation is taken as 9.1, and the sample size is 12. Substituting these values gives (106−100)/(9.1/√12)
para

t‑critical value lookup. For a two‑tailed test at the 0.05 significance level with 11 degrees of freedom the critical t value is 1.796. This value is obtained from the t‑distribution table using the specified alpha and degrees of freedom
para
computed t‑statistic. Using the sample data the t‑statistic is calculated as (106 − 100) ÷ (9.1 / √12) which equals 2.28. This value is larger than the critical value of 1.796
para
rejection region. The rejection region consists of t values whose absolute magnitude exceeds 1.796. Any computed statistic falling in this region leads to rejection of the null hypothesis
para
decision. Because 2.28 lies beyond the critical value, the null hypothesis is rejected at the 0.05 level
para

hypotheses interpretation. The null hypothesis states μ = 100, meaning eating walnuts causes no difference in IQ. The alternative hypothesis states μ ≠ 100, indicating a possible effect of walnuts on IQ

question.q: What does a Type I error represent in hypothesis testing?
question.answer: Rejecting the null hypothesis when it is actually true.
